title: system.v1
description:
How a site's runtime is configured and how much room it is using. An allowlist: anything absent is rejected, not ignored. Note what is not here — no paths, no file names, no directory listings, no configuration values beyond the handful of numeric limits below, and nothing about the content of anything measured. A byte count of an assets volume says how much is there; it says nothing about what.

Separate from inventory.v1 rather than added to it, and behind its own capability. Measuring disk means walking a directory tree, and sampling request timings means the connector observes traffic — both are a different kind of collection from reading a version number, so granting one must be a deliberate act rather than something an existing grant quietly starts doing.

collected_at.description: Unix timestamp at which the connector gathered this data.

storage.description: Sizes of the volumes Craft manages. Labels are a closed set, so a site cannot name a directory here and thereby report a path.

handle.description: The asset volume's handle. Not its path, and not its filesystem type.

measured.description: False when the volume could not be walked — remote storage, or a tree too large for the time budget. A size of zero and a size nobody could measure are different facts.

storage_bytes.description: Craft's own storage directory: logs, caches, compiled templates, backups it has taken itself.

php.description: Runtime limits, as numbers. Never phpinfo(), never a path, never an ini file, and never the value of any setting that could name one.

memory_limit_bytes.description: -1 where the limit is unlimited, which is a real setting and not an error.

extensions.description: Count only. The list itself would fingerprint the host in a way a byte count does not.

response.description: How long the site took to build its own responses, sampled on the site from traffic that was happening anyway. This is server processing time — the connector cannot see network, TLS or queueing — so it is not time to first byte and the interface does not call it that.
